about.title: About
about.text: I'm a design engineer. I started out in graphic design and typography, and later moved into building web apps, from the interface down to the database. I still care as much about how a product feels as how it works. That's where I help most: I turn design ideas into code without losing the details, and I make product choices with people in mind. On the side, I design typefaces and try out new ideas.

items.description: I build across a five-brand media platform on .NET and Next.js, from the database to the screen. I reworked PressRelease search so lookups went from seconds to milliseconds in local testing, built Nombase Funding end to end, and set up Sentry across 7 services.

I turned designs into production UI for nombase.com and the BevNET brands, keeping the details intact from design to code. The work grew from the front end into APIs, databases, migrations, and testing, which led to my promotion to Software Engineer.

I designed type and built the production tooling behind the typefaces, with Python scripts and Glyphs plugins. I also built the Branding System Generator and presented it at Typographics TypeLab 2022.
This is where art, design, and code came together for me. I built interactive front ends with generative art and animation, and automated editorial design by connecting Python and Pandas to InDesign.

I refreshed the visual language of the department's communications and built event branding systems, from merchandise and motion to editorial, type, web, and signage. Repetitive work like diplomas and animated invitations is what got me writing Python and JavaScript, and into software.
I spent over ten years in design before code. This is the archive of that work. Take a look.

projects.title: Projects
projects.heading: Where design meets code
projects.intro: I love the projects that live between design and code. Each one here taught me something new, whether it was a font tool, a payments portal or a marketplace on the blockchain. Open any card to see what I did and how it came to life.

eduardo-pavon.title: Eduardo Pavón
eduardo-pavon.summary: A gallery site for Eduardo Pavón, an artist who draws with Bic pens. Fast, bilingual and calm, so the drawings carry the page.
explanation: Eduardo Pavón builds hyperrealistic drawings stroke by stroke with a ballpoint pen. The site had to show that patience up close.
I built a static site in Spanish and English that loads fast and stays out of the way. A magnifier lets you follow every line.
highlights: Static pages in two languages, built with Astro and Tailwind, with no framework running in the browser.
One small script: a magnifier over each drawing.
An image pipeline that prepares every artwork for the web.
Everything runs in Docker, from the dev server to the build.

media.home: The home page: the artist’s name in big blue letters over a short statement about his work.
media.clip: A scroll down the home page, past the statement and into the drawings.

font-proofer.title: Font Proofer
font-proofer.summary: A Claude Code template for type designers. Drop in your fonts, answer a few questions, and get print proofs and web test pages.
explanation: Proofing a font usually means scripts, Python and a lot of setup. I wanted type designers to skip all of that.

You drop your fonts in a folder and talk to Claude in plain words. It reads the fonts, asks what you need and builds the proofs inside a container you never have to open. I presented it at TypeLab 2026.
highlights: Three specialists split the work: a typographer, a font engineer and a web engineer.
/init-font reads metrics, character coverage, languages, OpenType features and variable axes.
Vector PDF proofs with waterfalls, kerning tests and language specimens.
Fonts stay on your machine. They are never committed or uploaded.

media.title: The title slide of my TypeLab 2026 talk: a large serif “Aa” over “Claude Font Proofer”.
media.print: A slide about the print proof, with a screenshot of a generated PDF.
media.web: A slide about the web proof, with a screenshot of a live specimen.

vibe-coded-torus.title: Vibe-coded Torus
vibe-coded-torus.summary: The classic spinning ASCII torus, rebuilt in Rust as an experiment in working with Claude Code from a written spec.
explanation: donut.c draws a spinning 3D torus with nothing but text characters. I rebuilt it in Rust with Claude Code.
I wrote the math down first, then had every step covered by tests. The version below is a port that runs in your browser.
highlights: Samples points on the torus, rotates them, projects them and shades each one with 12 characters.
The math lives in its own spec, and tests cover projection, light and rendering.
Runs anywhere with one Docker command.
vibe-coded-torus.shareAlt: An ASCII torus drawn with text characters on black.

letrastica-5.title: Letrástica 5
letrastica-5.summary: The animated logo for Letrástica 5: letters with eyes that follow your pointer, over a field of restless little figures.
explanation: The logo for Letrástica’s fifth edition was drawn as a cast of characters with eyes. I didn’t design it. I animated it.
Each letter watches your pointer and blinks on its own, and the little figures around them keep moving. It was built to drop into the event’s site. Move your pointer over the one below.
highlights: Each letter is its own SVG drawing, with eyes that track the pointer, or your tap on a phone.
The eyes blink at their own pace, and the letters bounce a little out of step.
The little figures in the background jump around at random, so it never looks the same twice.
Built to slot into the event’s site as a self-contained piece.

media.desktop: The animated Letrástica 5 logo: black letters with white eyes on a bright green field of little figures.
media.phone: The logo stacked for a phone screen.

letrastica-5.shareAlt: The Letrástica 5 logo: black letters with white eyes on a bright green field of little figures.

the-session.title: The Session
the-session.summary: A DApp for finding a group therapy session and joining the talk. We built it as a team for ETHOnline 2023.
explanation: The Session started with a simple idea: talking helps, and nobody should feel alone with it.
Our designer shaped it in Figma, our smart contract developer wrote the contracts, and I built the app. Its warm, bold look made something hard feel welcoming.
highlights: A Next.js front end built from the team’s Figma design.
Messages between people through Push Protocol.
A contract deployed on Scroll’s Sepolia network.

media.clip: A scroll through the home page and its row of therapy groups.
media.groups: Session cards for anxiety, depression, stress management and grief, each with a day, time and number of peers.
media.phone: The home page on a phone.

the-session.shareAlt: The Session home page: “let’s talk about it” over a row of rounded session cards.

emoji-drop.title: Emoji Drop
emoji-drop.summary: A small DApp on the Internet Computer. Send an emoji and see which one people send the most.
explanation: A compact project to learn how the Internet Computer works.
A canister stores every emoji people send and counts them. The page shows the favorite.
highlights: A Motoko canister that counts emojis and checks that each input really is one.
A React and TypeScript front end served from the chain itself.

media.home: The Emoji Drop card: a field to pick an emoji, a Verify button and a round Send button.
media.phone: The top emoji section on a phone.

emoji-drop.shareAlt: The Emoji Drop card, with a field to pick an emoji and a Send button.

collectible-pleasures.title: Collectible Pleasures
collectible-pleasures.summary: A DApp that turns three letters into an NFT, drawn as the waves of the Unknown Pleasures cover. I built the art, the contract and the app.
explanation: A project from my Alchemy University bootcamp, and a tribute to the Unknown Pleasures album cover.

You type three letters, and each one becomes a stack of noisy waves. A small server draws the art and saves it to IPFS, and a contract mints it as an NFT. Try the generator below. To mint one, use the live site.
highlights: A full alphabet drawn only with waves: each letter is a set of wave modules.
The same art engine in Python, rendering animated GIFs.
A Solidity contract with tests, and a Next.js app to connect a wallet and mint.

media.home: The live site: “Collectible” over a square of white wave lines, then “PLEASURES” and a field to type three letters.
media.phone: The same page on a phone.

collectible-pleasures.shareAlt: Collectible Pleasures: a square of white wave lines between “Collectible” and “PLEASURES”.

melvin-pay.title: Melvin Pay
melvin-pay.summary: A payments product I helped bring to launch. I cleaned up the shared components so they were easier to work with and shipped the merchant-portal features the team needed to go live.
explanation: Melvin Pay let pet owners pay for vet visits and pet care in installments. I joined to help bring it to launch, and I built the merchant portal: the side that clinics and shops used to run their sales.
The company has since closed, so these screens come from my code running with made-up data.
highlights: A dashboard where a shop creates tickets and collects payments in one tap.
Ticket lists for pending, paid and unused sales, with the payment history of each one.
A weekly income report that splits cash, transfers and balances.
Shared components cleaned up so the team could ship faster.

media.clip: A walk through the merchant portal: the ticket tabs, then the weekly income report.

typefobia.title: Typefobia
typefobia.summary: The site for Typefobia, an “anti-congress” of type. Loud colors, a full program, and donations by card or crypto.
explanation: Typefobia was an irreverent type event, and the site had to match its tone.
With Letter Engine, I built the pages for the program, the guests and the workshops, plus a way to donate with PayPal or a crypto wallet. I wrote most of the code.
highlights: A Next.js site with pages for the program, guests, workshops and activities.
A donation contract in Solidity with tests, connected through a wallet button.
PayPal donations and a Mailchimp newsletter sign-up.

media.clip: A scroll down the home page as the gradient shifts.

fontfactory.title: FontFactory
fontfactory.summary: A NEAR DApp that mints your own copy of the Paradisio font, stamped with a unique font ID.
explanation: What if every copy of a font knew who owned it? FontFactory was my test of that idea on NEAR.
You sign in with a NEAR wallet and mint an instance of Paradisio with its own ID.
highlights: A Rust contract on NEAR’s testnet, with unit and integration tests.
A small front end that signs in with a NEAR wallet and shows the latest font ID.

media.home: The FontFactory page: a round FF logo, a box for the latest font ID and a NEAR sign-in button.
media.phone: The same page on a phone.

fontfactory.shareAlt: The FontFactory page with its round FF logo.

interplanetary-fonts.title: InterplanetaryFonts
interplanetary-fonts.summary: A decentralized marketplace for fonts that I co-designed. It reached the ETHOnline 2022 finals and joined the Women Build Web3 accelerator. I shaped the interface and the data behind it.
explanation: InterplanetaryFonts was a marketplace where type designers could share font projects, get funded while they work and sell fonts as NFTs.
We built it as a small team for ETHOnline 2022, where it reached the finals, and then took it into the Women Build Web3 accelerator. Our demo video shows the whole flow.
highlights: I built most of the hackathon front end: the gallery, the font pages and the creator profiles.
On a font page you pick the characters to mint, watch the price change, and test the font loaded from IPFS.
Modals to mint, fund a project, and stream payments to its creators with Superfluid.
In the accelerator I added Lens Protocol sign-in and profiles, and a GraphQL layer with Apollo.
I reworked the home page state and moved fonts and colors into shared CSS variables.

media.clip-demo: Our ETHOnline 2022 demo video, with sound.

ascii-name-generator.title: ASCII Name Generator
ascii-name-generator.summary: A Python program that writes your name in big ASCII letters, plus a little website that keeps every name it made.
explanation: One of my first coding projects, and still one of my favorites.
I drew a whole alphabet on a grid in Python, then wrote a program that builds any name from it. It can also fill each stroke with random letters. Type your name below.
highlights: A hand-drawn alphabet, seven rows tall, stored as simple grids.
A random mode that fills every stroke with different letters.
Every name made in the terminal shows up on the project’s website.

privacy.title: Privacy notice
privacy.intro: This page explains what this site collects about you, why, who else handles it, how long I keep it, and how to have it deleted. It describes how the site works today.

sections.title: Who I am
body: I'm Eduardo Aire Torres. I run this site on my own, and I'm responsible for the personal data it collects.
My address for legal notices is {address}. The fastest way to reach me is {email}.

sections.title: What I collect
body: When you send the contact form, I get:
Your name
Your email address
Your message
The language of the page you used
When you email me directly, I get your email address, your name if your email shows it, and what you write.
Like any website, the services that run this site also see technical details, such as your IP address and your browser. The sections below say who sees what.
I don't ask for sensitive data, such as your health, religion or political views. Please leave it out of your message.
You don't have to give me anything. Without a name, an email and a message, though, the form can't send and I can't reply.

sections.title: Why I use it
body: I use your name, email and message only to read your message and reply to you. I keep a backup copy so your message isn't lost if an email goes missing. I check each send with reCAPTCHA to keep out spam.
That's all. I don't use your data for marketing or advertising, and I don't sell it. Every use above is needed to answer you, so there are no optional uses to turn off.

reCAPTCHA gives each send a score. If the score is too low, the form doesn't send and asks you to try again or email me. A very high score also means you get a short "thanks" email. Nothing else about you is decided automatically.
If EU law applies to you, the legal basis is my legitimate interest in answering the messages people send me and keeping out spam (GDPR Article 6(1)(f)).

sections.title: Who else handles it
body: These companies help run the site. Each one gets only what it needs:

Amazon Web Services (AWS) delivers your message to my inbox through Amazon SES. When reCAPTCHA is very sure you're a person, SES also sends you a short "thanks" email that includes nothing you wrote. Amazon DynamoDB keeps the backup copy. {aws}

Google hosts my inbox in Google Workspace, so your name, email and message are stored there. Google reCAPTCHA checks that a person is using the form. It loads when you first click or tab into one of the form's fields, and it collects details about your browser and device for that check. {google}

Adobe serves the site's font on every page through Adobe Fonts. Your browser downloads the font from Adobe, so Adobe receives your IP address. Adobe says it doesn't store your IP address or set cookies, and that it counts which fonts each website uses so it can pay the type designers. {adobe}

Vercel hosts the site. Like any host, it receives your IP address and browser details when you open a page. It uses them to send you the page, block bots, and limit how often one IP address can send the form. {vercel}
I don't share your data with anyone else, unless a law or a court order requires it.

sections.title: Where it's stored
body: All four companies are based in the United States, so your data leaves Mexico. AWS keeps the backup copy in its us-east-1 region, in Virginia, USA. The other services may handle your data in the United States or in other countries where they have servers.

If you write from the European Union, your data goes to the United States. All four companies are certified under the EU-U.S. Data Privacy Framework, which the European Commission recognizes as giving adequate protection.

sections.title: How long I keep it
body: The backup copy: 90 days. After that date, DynamoDB deletes it on its own, usually within a few days.
Emails in my inbox: while we're in touch. I delete them when you ask me to.
The Vercel logs I can see: one hour. They never include what you wrote. Vercel may keep its own records longer, as its privacy notice explains.
reCAPTCHA data: as Google's terms describe.
Your theme choice: until you clear your browser's storage.
What you type into the project demos: until you close the tab.

sections.title: Cookies and browser storage
body: This site's code sets no cookies and uses no analytics or ad trackers.

Theme: the site saves "light" or "dark" in your browser's local storage, under the name "theme", so the page keeps its look on your next visit. On your first visit it saves your device's setting. It never leaves your device.

Project demos: the live pieces on some project pages (Collectible Pleasures and ASCII Name Generator) keep the letters you type, and the random-letters choice, in your browser's session storage, under the names "waves-letters", "ascii-name" and "ascii-random". They never leave your device and are deleted when you close the tab.

reCAPTCHA: when you use the contact form, Google sets a cookie called _GRECAPTCHA for its spam check. Because reCAPTCHA loads from google.com, your browser may also send Google cookies it already has for google.com.
Vercel: if Vercel shows you a short browser check, your browser remembers for one hour that you passed it.
You can clear or block these in your browser settings. If you block reCAPTCHA, the form can't send, so email me instead.

sections.title: How to limit what I get
body: Email me at {email} instead of using the form. Then no backup copy is saved, and reCAPTCHA doesn't load unless you click or tab into one of the form's fields.
Block third-party fonts in your browser. The site still works and uses a font from your device instead.
Ask me at any time to delete your messages, as explained below.

sections.title: Your rights
body: You can ask me to:
Show you the data I have about you, and send you a copy in a common format
Correct it
Delete it
Stop using it, or withdraw your consent

Email {email} from the address you used. Say what you'd like and, if you can, roughly when you wrote. If I can't tell the request is yours, I'll ask you to confirm it. It's free, and I'll answer and act on it within 20 business days. When I delete your data, I'll let you know.

sections.title: Complaints
body: If you're not happy with my answer, or you don't get one in time, you can complain:
In Mexico, to the {sabg}, within 15 business days of my answer, or once the 20 business days pass without one.
In the European Union, to the data protection authority of your country. The {edpb} lists them.

sections.title: Changes to this notice
body: If I change what the site collects or how I use it, I'll update this page and the date at the top when the change goes live.
